In mathematics, a '''regular element''' of a [[Lie algebra]] or [[Lie group]] is an element whose centralizer has dimension as small as possible.
For example, in a complex semisimple Lie algebra, an element <math>X \in \mathfrak{g}</math> is regular if its centralizer in <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> has dimension equal to the rank of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, which in turn equals the dimension of some Cartan subalgebra <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> (note that in earlier papers, an element of a complex semisimple Lie algebra was termed regular if it is semisimple and the kernel of its adjoint representation is a Cartan subalgebra).
An element <math> g \in G </math> a Lie group is regular if its centralizer has dimension equal to the rank of <math> G </math>.

== Basic case ==
In the specific case of <math>\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb{k})</math>, the Lie algebra of <math>n \times n </math> matrices over an [[algebraically closed field]] <math>\mathbb{k}</math> (such as the [[complex number]]s), a '''regular element''' <math>M</math> is an element whose [[Jordan normal form]] contains a single Jordan block for each eigenvalue (in other words, the geometric multiplicity of each eigenvalue is 1).
The centralizer of a regular element is the set of polynomials of degree less than <math>n</math> evaluated at the matrix <math>M</math>, and therefore the centralizer has dimension <math>n</math> (which equals the rank of <math>\mathfrak{gl}_n</math>, but is not necessarily an algebraic torus).

If the matrix <math>M</math> is diagonalisable, then it is regular [[if and only if]] there are <math>n</math> different eigenvalues. To see this, notice that <math>M</math> will commute with any matrix <math>P</math> that stabilises each of its eigenspaces. If there are <math>n</math> different eigenvalues, then this happens only if <math>P</math> is diagonalisable on the same basis as <math>M</math>; in fact <math>P</math> is a [[linear combination]] of the first <math>n</math> powers of <math>M</math>, and the centralizer is an [[algebraic torus]] of [[complex dimension]] <math>n</math> (real dimension <math>2n</math>); since this is the smallest possible dimension of a centralizer, the matrix <math>M</math> is regular. However if there are equal eigenvalues, then the centralizer is the product of the general linear groups of the eigenspaces of <math>M</math>, and has strictly larger dimension, so that <math>M</math> is not regular.  

For a connected [[compact Lie group]] <math>G</math>, the regular elements form an open [[Dense set|dense subset]], made up of <math>G</math>-[[conjugacy class]]es of the elements in a [[maximal torus]] <math>T</math> which are regular in <math>G</math>. The regular elements of <math>T</math> are themselves explicitly given as the complement of a set in <math>T</math>, a set of codimension-one subtori corresponding to the [[Semisimple Lie algebra#Cartan subalgebras and root systems|root system]] of <math>G</math>. Similarly, in the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> of <math>G</math>, the regular elements form an open dense subset which can be described explicitly as [[Adjoint representation|adjoint]] <math>G</math>-orbits of regular elements of the Lie algebra of <math>T</math>, the elements outside the hyperplanes corresponding to the root system.<ref>{{cite book |first=Mark R. |last=Sepanski |title=Compact Lie Groups |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=F3NgD_25OOsC&pg=PA156 |date=2006 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0-387-30263-8 |pages=156}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Let <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over an infinite field.<ref>Editorial note: the definition of a regular element over a finite field is unclear.</ref> For each <math>x \in \mathfrak{g}</math>, let
:<math>p_x(t) = \det(t - \operatorname{ad}(x)) = \sum_{i=0}^{\dim \mathfrak{g}} a_i(x) t^i</math>
be the [[characteristic polynomial]] of the [[adjoint endomorphism]] <math>\operatorname{ad}(x) : y \mapsto [x, y]</math> of <math>\mathfrak g</math>. Then, by definition, the '''rank''' of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is the least integer <math>r</math> such that <math>a_r(x) \ne 0</math> for some <math>x \in \mathfrak g</math> and is denoted by <math>\operatorname{rk}(\mathfrak{g})</math>.<ref name="Def">{{harvnb|Bourbaki|1981|loc=Ch. VII, § 2.2. Definition 2.}}</ref> For example, since <math>a_{\dim \mathfrak g}(x) = 1</math> for every ''x'', <math>\mathfrak g</math> is nilpotent (i.e., each <math>\operatorname{ad}(x)</math> is nilpotent by [[Engel's theorem]]) if and only if <math>\operatorname{rk}(\mathfrak{g}) = \dim \mathfrak g</math>. Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero{{clarify|I don't think we need alg closed here. See below.|date=February 2026}}, if <math>\mathfrak h</math> is a Cartan subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak g</math> then <math>\operatorname{rk}(\mathfrak{g}) = \dim \mathfrak h</math>; see  the section below.

Let <math>\mathfrak{g}_{\text{reg}} = \{ x \in \mathfrak{g} | a_{\operatorname{rk}(\mathfrak{g})} (x) \ne 0 \}</math>. By definition, a '''regular element''' of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is an element of the set <math>\mathfrak{g}_{\text{reg}}</math>.<ref name="Def" /> Since <math>a_{\operatorname{rk}(\mathfrak{g})}</math> is a polynomial function on <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, with respect to the [[Zariski topology]], the set <math>\mathfrak{g}_{\text{reg}}</math> is an open subset of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.

Over <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, <math>\mathfrak{g}_{\text{reg}}</math> is a connected set (with respect to the usual topology),<ref>{{harvnb|Serre|2001|loc=Ch. III, § 1. Proposition 1.}}</ref> but over <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, it is only a finite union of connected open sets.<ref>{{harvnb|Serre|2001|loc=Ch. III, § 6.}}</ref>

== A Cartan subalgebra and a regular element ==
Over an infinite field, a regular element can be used to construct a [[Cartan subalgebra]], a self-normalizing nilpotent subalgebra. Over a field of characteristic zero, this approach constructs all the Cartan subalgebras.

Given an element <math>x \in \mathfrak{g}</math>, let
:<math>\mathfrak{g}^0(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \ker(\operatorname{ad}(x)^n : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g})</math>
be the [[generalized eigenspace]] of <math>\operatorname{ad}(x)</math> for eigenvalue zero. It is a subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak g</math>.<ref>This is a consequence of the binomial-ish formula for ad.</ref> Note that <math>\dim \mathfrak{g}^0(x)</math> is the same as the (algebraic) multiplicity<ref>Recall that the [[geometric multiplicity]] of an eigenvalue of an endomorphism is the dimension of the eigenspace while the [[algebraic multiplicity]] of it is the dimension of the generalized eigenspace.</ref> of zero as an eigenvalue of <math>\operatorname{ad}(x)</math>; i.e., the least integer ''m'' such that <math>a_m(x) \ne 0</math> in the notation in {{slink||Definition}}. Thus, <math>\operatorname{rk}(\mathfrak g) \le \dim \mathfrak{g}^0(x)</math> and the equality holds if and only if <math>x</math> is a regular element.<ref name="Def" />

The statement is then that if <math>x</math> is a regular element, then <math>\mathfrak{g}^0(x)</math> is a Cartan subalgebra.<ref>{{harvnb|Bourbaki|1981|loc=Ch. VII, § 2.3. Theorem 1.}}</ref> Thus, <math>\operatorname{rk}(\mathfrak g)</math> is the dimension of at least some Cartan subalgebra; in fact, <math>\operatorname{rk}(\mathfrak g)</math> is the minimum dimension of a Cartan subalgebra. More strongly, over a field of characteristic zero (e.g., <math>\mathbb{R}</math> or <math>\mathbb{C}</math>),<ref name="application">{{harvnb|Bourbaki|1981|loc=Ch. VII, § 3.3. Theorem 2.}}</ref>
*every Cartan subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> has the same dimension; thus, <math>\operatorname{rk}(\mathfrak g)</math> is the dimension of an arbitrary Cartan subalgebra,
*an element ''x'' of <math>\mathfrak g</math> is regular if and only if <math>\mathfrak{g}^0(x)</math> is a Cartan subalgebra, and
*every Cartan subalgebra is of the form <math>\mathfrak{g}^0(x)</math> for some regular element <math>x \in \mathfrak g</math>.

== A regular element in a Cartan subalgebra of a complex semisimple Lie algebra ==
For a Cartan subalgebra <math>\mathfrak h</math> of a complex semisimple Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g</math> with the root system <math>\Phi</math>, an element of <math>\mathfrak h</math> is regular if and only if it is not in the union of hyperplanes <math display="inline">\bigcup_{\alpha \in \Phi} \{ h \in \mathfrak{h} \mid \alpha(h) = 0 \}</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Procesi|2007|loc=Ch. 10, § 3.2.}}</ref> This is because: for <math>r = \dim \mathfrak h</math>,
*For each <math>h \in \mathfrak{h}</math>, the characteristic polynomial of <math>\operatorname{ad}(h)</math> is {{nowrap|<math display="inline">t^r \left(t^{\dim \mathfrak g - r} - \sum_{\alpha \in \Phi} \alpha(h) t^{\dim \mathfrak g - r - 1} + \cdots \pm \prod_{\alpha \in \Phi} \alpha(h)\right)</math>.}}

This characterization is sometimes taken as the definition of a regular element (especially when only regular elements in Cartan subalgebras are of interest).
